title: Microsoft AI chief Suleyman warns: AI is crossing a dangerous threshold; before alignment, it must first be containable

content_html:
On one side, AI is cracking extremely difficult math problems; on the other, it is escaping sandboxes, exploiting vulnerabilities, and requesting permissions in safety tests. Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman believes that the emergence of both types of signs at the same time means the AI industry “is crossing a threshold.” On November 25, he posted a warning on X: safety and alignment research must be prioritized and can no longer be delayed.

The threshold means “being unable to control it”

Based on the context of the tweet, this threshold refers to AI capabilities being about to cross the boundary of what humans can effectively supervise, control, and safely deploy. Specifically, when AI starts autonomously discovering vulnerabilities, carrying out operations across systems, hiding its true reasoning, and even learning to evade safety guardrails, the industry can no longer cling to the idea of “deal with it once it gets smarter.” It must first put safety and alignment mechanisms in place and contain the risks before capabilities grow.

First contain, then align

Suleyman’s argument has two steps: before true “alignment” can be achieved, “containment” must come first, meaning ensuring that humans can always constrain a model’s capabilities. Alignment (AI alignment) is a core concept in AI safety. It means making an AI system’s goals, behavior, and judgments align with the intentions, values, and rules of its designers and human society.

This warning comes against the backdrop of the Riemann Hypothesis proof incident combined with multiple AI safety testing incidents: in mathematics, AI has demonstrated its ability to crack extremely difficult problems; in testing, it has also exposed real risks such as breaking out of sandboxes, exploiting vulnerabilities, and gaining permissions. As capabilities and risks rise together, guardrails must keep pace first.
